planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade in spring once soil is workable.

directions: This selection of male fern grows in a distinctly narrow, upright, almost columnar vase shape rather than the broader spreading habit of the species, making it useful for tight shaded corners and narrow border edges. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and keep evenly moist during the first growing season to establish a strong crown. It shares the species' toughness and tolerance of dry shade and urban conditions once established. Groom by cutting back tattered fronds in late winter before new fiddleheads emerge.

planting.note: Set out divisions in cool, moist, humus-rich shaded soil in spring; give this finer-textured cultivar a bit more shelter than the species.

directions: A finely dissected, lace-like male fern selection with narrow pinnae and forked, crested (polydactyl) frond tips that give it a much softer, more delicate look than the coarse-textured species. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; it is somewhat less vigorous than plain male fern and benefits from a organic mulch to conserve moisture around the crown. Divide congested clumps in early spring, and remove old fronds before new croziers unfurl to keep the crest display clean. Best sited where its intricate frond texture can be appreciated up close, such as along a shaded path.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade with high humidity; grow as a container or houseplant outside zones 10-12.

directions: A larger, more vigorous selection of delta maidenhair noted for the faint, sweet fragrance released from its new fronds when brushed or lightly crushed, in addition to the classic fan-shaped bright-green leaflets on wiry black stems. It demands the same consistent moisture and high humidity as the species and will scorch quickly in dry air or direct sun. Outdoors it is hardy only in sheltered, humid zone 10-12 sites; elsewhere grow it as a prized houseplant or shaded patio container specimen, misting regularly and keeping it away from drafts and heat vents. Repot in spring as roots fill the container, dividing crowded clumps at that time.

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich potting mix in bright shade; this compact cultivar is the most commonly sold maidenhair for indoor culture.

directions: This is the most widely produced commercial maidenhair fern cultivar, valued for a naturally compact, dense habit and somewhat greater tolerance of average indoor humidity than the straight species, though it still requires consistent moisture and will drop leaflets quickly if allowed to dry out. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light or deep outdoor shade in zones 10-12. Mist regularly, keep away from cold drafts and forced-air heat registers, and trim off browned fronds at the base to keep new growth looking fresh. Divide and repot every year or two as the crown fills its container.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil or on a shaded rock crevice or log in spring.

directions: An old, RHS Award of Garden Merit-winning selection of the common polypody grown for its unusually variable, finely divided to almost feathery fronds, some plants in a batch producing broad segments and others tassel-like or plumose forms. Like the species it is an epiphytic-leaning, creeping-rhizome fern that thrives tucked into shaded rock crevices, atop moss-covered logs, or in humus-rich woodland soil with excellent drainage, and it tolerates considerable summer dryness once established. Foliage is evergreen and leathery, giving winter interest when little else is green in the shade garden. Top-dress lightly with leaf mold each fall rather than burying the shallow creeping rhizomes.

planting.note: Set shallow rhizome divisions into gritty, well-drained, humus-rich soil or a shaded rock ledge in spring.

directions: A historic crested form of the common polypody in which each frond segment and the frond tip repeatedly forks, giving a bristly, forked-tassel appearance distinct from the plain-fronded species. Culture matches wild polypody exactly: a shallow, creeping rhizome that prefers to run along the surface of humus-rich, gritty, well-drained soil, atop rocks, or over old stumps rather than being deeply buried. It is drought-tolerant once established and stays evergreen through winter, making it a useful textural accent for shaded rock gardens or woodland edges. Avoid heavy mulch over the rhizome, which can cause rot; a light leaf-litter top-dressing is preferable.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give plants room to develop their upright, arching vase form.

directions: This Japanese species forms a tidy, upright-arching clump of glossy, dark-green, twice-cut fronds with distinctively diamond-shaped, glossy leaflets, and new fronds often emerge with a silvery sheen before darkening. It is evergreen to semi-evergreen and, like other Polystichum, tolerant of drier shade than many woodland ferns once its root system is established, though best growth comes with steady moisture and rich organic soil. Combine it with hostas and hellebores for contrasting leaf texture in a shaded border. Remove tattered old fronds in late winter just before new croziers unfurl.

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; protect from frost outside its hardiness range.

directions: A robust New Zealand hard fern that forms large, coarse-textured colonies of long, leathery fronds, with new growth emerging in striking shades of pink, bronze, and copper before maturing to deep green. It spreads steadily by rhizomes to form dense groundcover-like stands in consistently moist, humus-rich, shaded sites, and tolerates boggy soil far better than most ferns. Growth is fastest and lushest with abundant moisture and shelter from drying wind; it is not reliably frost-hardy and needs zone 9-11 conditions or greenhouse protection in colder climates. Thin congested colonies periodically to maintain the bold new-growth color display.

planting.note: Plant crowns or divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; less aggressive than common ostrich fern so it suits smaller beds.

directions: Native to East Asia and sometimes classified as Pentarhizidium orientale, this relative of the common ostrich fern produces a similar upright, shuttlecock-shaped crown of finely cut, arching sterile fronds around shorter, dark fertile fronds, but at a smaller overall scale and with a far less aggressively running rhizome. This makes it a good choice for gardeners who want the classic ostrich-fern silhouette without the vigorous colonizing spread of Matteuccia struthiopteris. Grow in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; it will not tolerate drought. Foliage dies back to the ground in fall and re-emerges as tightly coiled fiddleheads in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a pond edge or boggy border.

directions: A crested selection of royal fern in which the tips of both the sterile fronds and the tall, rust-colored fertile spore clusters split and fork into tufted, tassel-like ends, adding ornamental texture to the already handsome, coarsely divided, locust-like foliage of the species. Culture is identical to plain royal fern: give it constantly moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil at a pond margin, stream bank, or rain garden in partial shade, where it will tolerate standing water better than almost any other fern. It is somewhat less vigorous and slightly shorter than the straight species, so site it where its crested display is visible up close. Foliage turns an attractive golden-bronze in fall before dying back for winter.
